extracted.intended_audience: AI researchers, safety engineers, red teamers, deployment teams, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and deployment guidance for large language models (GPT-4): measuring safety risks (hallucinations, harmful content, bias, privacy, cybersecurity, etc.), running qualitative and quantitative evaluations (red teaming, classifiers, human analysis), and applying model- and system-level mitigations (fine-tuning, refusals, monitoring, policies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative evaluations / expert red-teaming
rubrics_metrics.description: Use external experts to qualitatively probe, adversarially test, and provide feedback on model behavior (referred to informally as 'redteaming').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Redteaming should include stress-testing, boundary testing, and iterative rounds; select experts across fairness, alignment, dis/misinformation, chemistry, biorisk, cybersecurity, nuclear risks, economics, HCI, law, education, and healthcare. Acknowledge selection biases (e.g., English-speaking, Western countries) and that this process is informative but not comprehensive. Iteratively update mitigations based on findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative evaluations against content policy categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Build internal quantitative evaluations that measure the likelihood of a model generating content that falls into targeted content-policy categories (e.g., hate speech, self-harm advice, illicit advice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use classifiers plus human analysis to label generated text; automate evaluations to accelerate checkpoint comparison; target high-risk content areas and use these metrics to prioritize mitigation work and to compare model checkpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement of hallucinations (closed-domain and open-domain)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the model’s tendency to ‘hallucinate’ — produce content that is nonsensical or untruthful in relation to sources — using closed-domain and open-domain evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closed-domain hallucinations: evaluate when model should rely only on provided context but invents extra information (e.g., summaries containing facts not present). Open-domain hallucinations: model confidently provides false information without a specific input context. Use automatic evaluations (zero-shot classifiers) and human evaluations; construct factual and non-factual datasets. Report comparative improvements (e.g., percentage-point gains vs prior models).

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmful content categories to measure and mitigate
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and measure categories of harmful content the model can generate, including advice or encouragement for self-harm, graphic erotic or violent content, harassing/demeaning/hateful content, content useful for planning attacks or violence, and instructions for finding illegal content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on content areas that pose potential for harm regardless of context; use qualitative examples and quantitative classifiers; employ refusals and other mitigations to reduce generation of these content types. Examples in the report illustrate where GPT-4-early produced harmful completions and how mitigations changed outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harms of representation, allocation, and quality-of-service
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how models reinforce social biases and stereotypes (representation harms), create disparate outcomes in allocation of opportunities/resources (allocative harms), and produce uneven quality-of-service across demographics or languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure performance across different demographic groups and languages; be cautious using models in high-stakes decision contexts (e.g., law enforcement, criminal justice, migration, legal/health advice). Note that mitigation strategies like refusals can both reduce some harms and exacerbate disparities (e.g., unequal refusal behavior across demographics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overreliance and user trust risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess risk that users will overtrust the model’s outputs; hallucinations and increased model persuasiveness raise the danger of overreliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how increased coherence and truthfulness in some areas can paradoxically increase overall risk by encouraging trust in incorrect outputs; when models are integrated into systems, hallucinations may degrade information quality. Measurement and mitigations should aim to reduce misleadingly confident false outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy and identification risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the model’s potential to identify private individuals or reveal sensitive information, particularly when augmented with outside data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with experts to probe these risks; mitigation and monitoring are needed to limit the model’s ability to surface private information. This is an area requiring further robust evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cybersecurity and lowering of attack costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether model capabilities lower the cost or increase the ease of cyberattacks (e.g., enhancing social engineering, producing vulnerable code, finding sites selling illicit goods/services).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitatively and qualitatively evaluate outputs for cyber-risk content; consider mitigations like refusals, content filtering, and monitoring. Recognize that even modest capability gains can change attack economics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinformation and influence-operation risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the model’s potential to generate or amplify disinformation and to be used in influence operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure susceptibility to generating persuasive but false narratives; evaluate how model outputs might be used at scale for coordination or manipulation. Use diverse adversarial tests to probe such failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proliferation of conventional and unconventional weapons
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess risk that the model can generate content facilitating the proliferation or misuse of weapons, including technical instructions or synthesis procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include domain experts (e.g., chemistry, biosecurity) in red teams; use classifiers and refusals to block or reduce such outputs; document examples and track mitigation effectiveness over model versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for risky emergent behaviors and interactions with other systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Probe the possibility that models exhibit new, unanticipated capabilities or behaviors when scaled or when interacting with external systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct specialized tests (e.g., ARC evaluations) to explore autonomous-gathering or replication behaviors; iterate mitigations and monitor for emergent failure modes; treat speculative risks seriously and invest in further research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic impacts and acceleration risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider and evaluate macro-scale impacts such as labor-market effects, acceleration of capabilities, and economic externalities driven by deployment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage economists and domain experts to assess broader societal impacts; treat these considerations as part of deployment planning and governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model mitigation standards: dataset curation and training interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply model-level mitigations such as reducing prevalence of policy-violating content in pre-training data, fine-tuning with supervised data and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), and reducing tendencies to hallucinate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fine-tune on labeler demonstrations and use RLHF to align outputs with human preferences; leverage data from prior model usage to reduce adversarial prompt surface area; evaluate mitigation effectiveness quantitatively and qualitatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model refusals and instruction filtering
rubrics_metrics.description: Train models to refuse certain instructions (e.g., direct requests for illicit advice) as a mitigation against producing harmful content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refusal training can be effective for leading, explicit harmful prompts but may create false assurance or exacerbate bias/disparate service (unequal refusal across demographics). Monitor refusal behavior for fairness and coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring, classifiers, and system-level enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Deploy a range of classifiers and monitoring tools for new risk vectors and incorporate them into the operational monitoring workflow to enforce API usage policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine automated classifiers with human review; use monitoring to detect policy violations, inform enforcement, and guide further mitigations. Continuously update classifiers as new risk modes are discovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usage policy and access control restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Define and enforce usage policies that prohibit certain high-risk applications (e.g., high-risk government decision-making, certain legal/health advice contexts) and control access to models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply policy-based prohibitions together with technical controls, monitoring, and enforcement; communicate explicit prohibitions in documentation and terms of use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of performance disparities across languages and demographics
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure differential performance (e.g., decreased performance for speakers of some languages) and the resulting disparities in quality of service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include multilingual benchmarks and demographic analyses in evaluations; address disparities via data collection, targeted mitigations, and careful deployment constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stress testing and boundary testing procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use stress-testing and boundary-testing methods to surface edge cases and potential failure modes that might cause harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement red-teaming with stress and boundary tests focused on edge cases; iterate mitigations and retest to ensure fixes hold across new adversarial strategies.
